title: Two Fathoms: the Pilot, the Comet, and the Book He Called His Best
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Florida, Missouri: the comet's fortnight
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pool's coordinate was wrong twice over and is corrected here from Wikipedia, 'Florida, Missouri'
stops.campa: Halley's Comet passes perihelion on the sixteenth of November. Two weeks later, in a rented frame house in the hamlet of Florida, Monroe County, Missouri, Jane Lampton Clemens bears her sixth child, two months premature. John Marshall Clemens, storekeeper and sometime justice of the peace, names him Samuel Langhorne. The village holds a hundred people or so and no future. Seventy-four years on, the boy will announce that he intends to leave with the comet he arrived on, and he will be right to within a day.
suggested_refs: The two-room frame house at Florida, Missouri, now enclosed within the Mark Twain Birthplace State Historic Site
sources: Albert Bigelow Paine, Mark Twain: A Biography (1912)

stops.name: Hannibal: the family comes to the river
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: The Clemenses give up the inland hamlet and move east to Hannibal, a Mississippi port where the steamboats tie up twice a day and the levee is the whole economy. Sam is four. The town hands him the raft, the island, the cave, the whitewashed fence, the drowned men fished out below the bend, and the runaway hiding in the woods across the water. He will spend forty years converting it into a place called St. Petersburg, and the conversion consists mostly of changing the names.
stops.quote: When I was a boy, there was but one permanent ambition among my comrades in our village on the west bank of the Mississippi River. That was, to be a steamboatman.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi (1883), ch. 4 (Project Gutenberg ebook #245)
suggested_refs: The Clemens house on Hill Street, Hannibal, now the Mark Twain Boyhood Home and Museum
sources: Mark Twain Boyhood Home and Museum, Hannibal

stops.name: McDowell's Cave: the hill with a hole in it
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the pool dates the boyhood visits only as c. 1845-1852
stops.campa: Two miles south of town a limestone bluff above the river road opens into miles of branching passage. The Hannibal boys go in with candles and come out again, and the town keeps its stories about the ones who take a wrong turning. A local physician is said to keep a body preserved in alcohol in one of the chambers. This is the cave where Tom and Becky will lose the thread of the picnic crowd, and where Injun Joe will starve against a door that somebody else has locked from the outside.
suggested_refs: McDowell's Cave, south of Hannibal, renamed Mark Twain Cave
sources: Local tradition recorded at Mark Twain Cave

stops.name: Hannibal: the father dies and the boy is bound to the case
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded in the reachable sources
stops.campa: John Marshall Clemens dies of pneumonia, leaving debts, a worthless Tennessee land claim, and a widow with children to place. Sam leaves school after the fifth grade and is bound apprentice to a printer. By 1851 he is setting type for the Hannibal Journal, the paper his older brother Orion owns and cannot make pay, and slipping unsigned squibs into it when Orion is out of town. The trade will carry him across the country and back: a compositor can always eat, and a compositor learns words by their weight in metal.
suggested_refs: Surviving numbers of Orion Clemens's Hannibal Journal, 1851-1853

segments.name: The Type Case and the Pilot House

stops.name: New York: the journeyman printer
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded
stops.campa: At about eighteen he leaves Hannibal for good and works the type cases of New York, Philadelphia, St. Louis and Cincinnati in turn, a journeyman compositor carrying a card in the International Typographical Union. The card is the first thing he owns that a stranger in a strange city will honor. He sets other men's sentences for a living and begins, in the intervals, to place his own in country papers, where they are printed for nothing and read by no one he knows.
suggested_refs: The International Typographical Union card of Samuel L. Clemens, journeyman compositor

stops.name: Keokuk: Orion's shop, and a scheme for the Amazon
stops.date_confidence: June 1855 to about October 1856; the pool's range of 1855-1857 contradicted its own Cincinnati entry and is shortened here
stops.campa: Orion has moved his press up the river to Keokuk, Iowa, and Sam sets type for him there through a year and a half of thin wages. In the winter of 1856 he goes down to Cincinnati, boards on Walnut Street, and plans in earnest to sail for the headwaters of the Amazon and make a fortune in coca. He gets as far as a New Orleans steamboat before discovering that no vessel is going to South America, and that the money for the passage would not have covered it anyway.
suggested_refs: Orion Clemens's Keokuk print shop; the Walnut Street boarding house, Cincinnati

stops.name: New Orleans: the cub pilot under Bixby
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the date of the licence itself is absent from this pool
stops.campa: Instead of the Amazon he asks Horace E. Bixby to teach him the river. For two years he learns twelve hundred miles of shifting bottom by heart, upstream and down, in daylight and in dead black night, every crossing and bar and cottonwood snag committed to memory and then committed again when the water moves it, and he takes out his pilot's licence. New Orleans is the southern end of every run. He will say afterwards that it was the only trade he ever practised in which he was the complete master of the thing under him.
stops.quote: Whoo-oop! I'm the old original iron-jawed, brass-mounted, copper-bellied corpse-maker from the wilds of Arkansaw! Look at me! I'm the man they call Sudden Death and General Desolation! Sired by a hurricane, dam'd by an earthquake, half-brother to the cholera, nearly related to the small-pox on the mother's side!
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi (1883), ch. 3, the raftsman's boast (Project Gutenberg ebook #245)
suggested_refs: The New Orleans levee, southern terminus of the St. Louis runs
sources: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi (1883)

stops.name: Memphis: Henry, eight days after the boilers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pool carried the explosion date, 13 June, as the death date
stops.campa: Sam has found his younger brother Henry a berth on the Pennsylvania. On the thirteenth of June, above Memphis, four of her boilers let go and the steamboat burns to the waterline. Henry is thrown clear and scalded through; he is carried to a makeshift ward in Memphis and dies there eight days later, twenty years old. Sam, travelling a day behind on another boat, arrives in time to sit with him and not in time for anything else. He will carry the death as a thing he did.
suggested_refs: The wreck of the steamboat Pennsylvania, exploded above Memphis, 13 June 1858

stops.name: Marion County: two weeks of the Confederate army
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month approximate; no lens supplies a coordinate for the company's ground, so the county seat stands in
stops.campa: The war stops the river traffic, and the piloting with it. In the summer he joins a dozen or so Missouri irregulars who call themselves the Marion Rangers, is elected second lieutenant, drills in the rain, retreats from rumors of Union cavalry, and goes home when the company dissolves. It is the whole of his war and it lasts about two weeks. Meanwhile Orion has been appointed secretary of Nevada Territory and needs somebody to share the stagecoach and carry the bags.
suggested_refs: The Marion Rangers, an informal Confederate company raised in Marion County, Missouri, summer 1861

stops.name: Virginia City: two fathoms, water enough to pass
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He crosses the plains by stagecoach with Orion, settles at Carson City, digs the Comstock Lode without ever striking pay, and lets a campfire get away from him on the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe, burning off the timber claim he has just staked. Broke, he takes a reporter's desk at the Territorial Enterprise. On the third of February he signs a sketch with a leadsman's cry off the Mississippi: mark twain, two fathoms, water enough to pass. Samuel Clemens will publish almost nothing under his own name again.
suggested_refs: The Territorial Enterprise office, C Street, Virginia City, Nevada

stops.name: San Francisco: the Morning Call
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded
stops.campa: He comes over the Sierra and writes for the Morning Call, then for the Golden Era and the Californian, keeping company with Bret Harte and the rest of the city's literary bohemians. The Call work is drudgery, three columns a day of police court and fire alarm, and he says so in print. In the same streets in the same years Eadweard Muybridge is selling landscape views signed Helios, and has not yet been asked whether a running horse ever has all four feet off the ground.
suggested_refs: The San Francisco Morning Call office, Montgomery Street, 1864

stops.name: Angels Camp: the frog full of shot
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded; the publication date, 18 November 1865, is attested to the day
stops.campa: Rained into a mining camp in Calaveras County, he listens to an old man tell, at enormous length and with perfect gravity, how a stranger filled a champion jumping frog with quail shot. He writes it down in his notebook. The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County runs in the New York Saturday Press on the eighteenth of November and is reprinted across the country inside a month. The name out of the Nevada sagebrush is suddenly national, and the man carrying it is thirty years old.
suggested_refs: The Angels Hotel bar-room, Angels Camp, where the frog story was told

stops.name: Kilauea: the crater by torchlight
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month approximate
stops.campa: The Sacramento Union sends him to the Sandwich Islands and prints the letters he sends back. He rides across Hawaii to the crater of Kilauea and stands over the lake of fire at night with a torch in his hand, and writes that nothing he has seen in his life stands anywhere near it. The islands give him four months and a book's worth of copy. They also give him the discovery that a man who can write a comic paragraph can stand up in front of a paying room and say it out loud.
suggested_refs: The Sacramento Union dispatches of 1866, later collected as Letters from Hawaii
sources: Mark Twain, Letters from Hawaii (Sacramento Union dispatches, 1866)

stops.name: Tangier: the first sight of Africa
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded; the ship sailed from New York on 8 June 1867
stops.campa: The steamship Quaker City clears New York on the eighth of June with a load of pilgrims, a chaplain, and one newspaper correspondent under contract to be funny about them. She makes her first landfall at Horta in the Azores, then anchors under the Rock of Gibraltar. A shore party crosses to Tangier, and Twain stands for the first time in Africa and in an entirely Muslim city: not one square corner, not one straight street, nothing built to any measure he was raised to expect.
suggested_refs: The steamship Quaker City, chartered for the 1867 excursion to Europe and the Holy Land

stops.name: Paris: the Exposition Universelle
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: The excursion lands its passengers at Marseille and goes up to Paris, where the machines of the world are on show at the Exposition Universelle and every guide in the city is called Ferguson because Twain refuses to learn their names. He walks the whole tourist circuit with a straight face and files copy that mocks the circuit rather than the city. The letters home are already a book: The Innocents Abroad, published in 1869, will make him the best-known humorist in America.
suggested_refs: The Paris Exposition Universelle of 1867

stops.name: Rome: the Old Masters and the guides
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded; Naples and Pompeii follow in August
stops.campa: At Milan he climbs the cathedral roof and stands in front of the ruin of Leonardo's Last Supper; at Venice he rides the gondolas and declines to be moved. In Rome he does the Colosseum, the Vatican and the catacombs, and works up the joke that carries the whole book. The Old Masters are not sacred and the guides are frauds. A man who reports that he was moved when he was not is lying for the sake of Europe. In August he climbs Vesuvius and walks the excavated streets of Pompeii.
suggested_refs: The plaster casts of the dead at Pompeii, described in The Innocents Abroad

stops.name: Constantinople: the bazaars, after the Parthenon by night
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: Held offshore at Athens under quarantine, Twain and three companions row ashore in the dark, walk up past the guards, stand alone in the Parthenon by moonlight, rob a vineyard on the way down and are back aboard before dawn. The ship then works the Black Sea: Sevastopol still in ruins a dozen years after the siege, an audience with Tsar Alexander II at Livadia, Odessa so like an American town that he is briefly homesick. At Constantinople he walks the bazaars and the converted cathedral of Hagia Sophia.
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia; the Livadia Palace audience with Alexander II, August 1867

stops.name: Damascus: the Street called Straight
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: The pilgrims land at Beirut and ride inland. In Damascus, the oldest continuously inhabited city on earth, Twain walks the Street called Straight and goes down with a fever that nearly ends the trip for him. A few streets away, in the Amara quarter, Emir Abdelkader is teaching Ibn Arabi to a circle of students and has been living in the city twelve years; seven summers earlier he stood armed in the Christian quarter and pulled thousands of strangers out of a massacre. Neither man is told the other is in the city.
suggested_refs: The Street called Straight, Damascus; the emir's house in the Amara quarter

stops.name: Jerusalem: the least reverent pilgrim on the road
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded; the pin is the atlas's canonical Temple Mount coordinate
stops.campa: The party rides down through Galilee, where Twain measures the lake against the pilgrims' rhapsodies and finds it small. He comes into Jerusalem on horseback, walks the Church of the Holy Sepulchre with his hat off and his skepticism intact, and stands on the esplanade that Abraham's story fixes, that Hadrian plowed under and rebuilt as a Roman forum, and that al-Kamil handed to Frederick by treaty in 1229. The pilgrims rejoin the ship at Jaffa. He will publish the least reverent American book yet written about this ground.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre; the Temple Mount esplanade, canonical pin of the atlas

stops.name: Giza: the face that gets past his guard
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: At the end of the voyage the party crosses to Egypt. Twain is pushed and hauled up the courses of the Great Pyramid by guides who want a coin at every block, and sits afterwards in front of the Sphinx, which he describes without a single joke in it: a face looking out over nothing in particular, patient and remembering. It is the one monument of the whole tour he does not make fun of. The Quaker City turns for home carrying a young passenger, Charles Langdon, who has shown him an ivory miniature of his sister.
suggested_refs: The Sphinx passage of The Innocents Abroad, ch. 58

stops.name: Buffalo: a third share of the Express
stops.date_confidence: 1869 attested for the purchase of the share; month approximate
stops.campa: Engaged, and needing a trade that keeps him in one place, Twain buys a third share of the Buffalo Express and begins writing editorials for it. Jervis Langdon, without telling either of them, buys the couple a furnished house on Delaware Avenue and keeps the deed in his pocket until the wedding journey ends at its door. The Buffalo years will hold a newspaper, a house, a son born ailing, and two funerals, and will be over inside eighteen months of beginning.
suggested_refs: The Delaware Avenue house, Buffalo; Twain's share in the Buffalo Express, 1869-1871

stops.name: Elmira: the wedding in the Langdon house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the geography lens placed this wedding in Buffalo and is wrong
stops.campa: On the second of February, in her father's house on Main Street, Samuel Clemens marries Olivia Louise Langdon, whose portrait he was shown in a stateroom in the Mediterranean two and a half years before. Jervis Langdon, coal magnate and abolitionist, has made inquiries about the bridegroom's character, received answers ranging from lukewarm to alarming, and given him the daughter anyway. The marriage will last thirty-four years and end in a rented villa outside Florence.
suggested_refs: The Langdon family house, Main Street, Elmira, New York

stops.name: Buffalo: the boy who does not last
stops.date_confidence: year attested for Langdon Clemens's birth; month and day unrecorded in this pool
stops.campa: Their son Langdon is born in the Delaware Avenue house, small and ailing from the first week. Inside two years the boy is dead of diphtheria at nineteen months, and the Clemenses have sold the house, sold the share in the Express, and left Buffalo for good. Susy is born at Elmira in the same year that Langdon dies. The family's arithmetic from here forward runs in two columns, the children living and the children buried, and the second column keeps gaining.
suggested_refs: The grave of Langdon Clemens, died 2 June 1872, Woodlawn Cemetery, Elmira

stops.name: Hartford: the house on Farmington Avenue
stops.date_confidence: occupancy year attested; the pool wrongly dated the Hartford move to 1873, against renting from 1871 and buying land in 1873
stops.campa: The family has rented at Nook Farm since 1871, a Hartford neighborhood of writers and reformers; in 1873 they buy land on Farmington Avenue and set Edward Tuckerman Potter to build. What goes up is twenty-five rooms of High Victorian Gothic, brick laid in three colors, balconies on every face of it, a glassed conservatory, and a billiard room under the roof where he works. They move in in 1874 and stay seventeen years. It is the longest settled address of his life and it will nearly be demolished.
suggested_refs: 351 Farmington Avenue, Hartford, built 1874 by Edward Tuckerman Potter
sources: The Mark Twain House and Museum

stops.name: Quarry Farm: the octagonal study in the field
stops.date_confidence: the study is attested as built by the Cranes in 1874; the pool's coordinate was 2.5 km south of the farm and is corrected
stops.campa: On the hill above Elmira, at his sister-in-law Susan Crane's farm, the family takes the summer. In 1874 the Cranes build him a study out in the field, octagonal and glazed on every side like a pilot house, far enough from the door that nobody can call him in to meals. He works there through the hot months for the better part of thirty years. Most of Tom Sawyer, published in 1876, most of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, and Life on the Mississippi are drafted in it. Hartford is where he lives; this is where the books get written.
suggested_refs: The octagonal study at Quarry Farm, built 1874, moved to the Elmira College campus in 1952
sources: Center for Mark Twain Studies, Elmira College

stops.name: Heidelberg: the tramp abroad
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded
stops.campa: He takes the family to Europe and starts from Heidelberg, walking the Neckar valley with his Hartford minister Joseph Twichell and then the Alps, where the two of them stage a mock scientific expedition across the Gorner Glacier and compute with great solemnity how many centuries the ice will take to deliver them to the valley floor. Out of the walk comes A Tramp Abroad, with an appendix on the awful German language proposing reforms that no German has requested.
suggested_refs: The Gorner Glacier expedition, A Tramp Abroad (1880), and its appendix on the German language

stops.name: Quarry Farm: Jean, the last of the four
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the chronology lens gave the birthplace as Hartford and is wrong
stops.campa: Jean Clemens is born at Quarry Farm on the twenty-sixth of July, the fourth and last child. The household is Olivia and three daughters now: Susy at eight, Clara at six, Jean in the cradle, with the infant Langdon eight years dead. Jean will develop epilepsy in her teens, spend years in treatment away from her family, and die at twenty-nine on a Christmas Eve in her father's last house. Of the four children only Clara will outlive him, and she will bury the rest of them in one plot.
suggested_refs: Quarry Farm, Elmira, birthplace of Jean Clemens, 26 July 1880

stops.name: Hartford: the twelve years of reading begin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, back-counted from Twain's own claim of twelve years of preparation before the 1895 serialization; no document dates the start
stops.campa: He begins reading toward a book about Joan of Arc and will read for twelve years before he writes a line of it: Quicherat's edition of the trial, the rehabilitation depositions of 1456, the chronicles, in French and in English both. What he is reading includes the villagers of Domremy testifying about the beech on the Vaucouleurs road, the Fairy Tree of the Bourlemonts, where Pierre de Bourlemont's lady picnicked with the children and where Joffrey Bourlemont sank a well in his grief, and around which Joan was accused of dancing.
stops.quote: To arrive at a just estimate of a renowned man's character one must judge it by the standards of his time, not ours.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc (1896), Translator's Preface, opening sentence (Project Gutenberg ebook #2874)
suggested_refs: Jules Quicherat, Proces de condamnation et de rehabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc (1841-1849)

sources: Wikipedia, 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: Hartford: Huckleberry Finn
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the first edition appeared in Britain in December 1884 and in America in February 1885
stops.campa: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is published, eight years after Tom Sawyer and after two long abandonments of the manuscript, and libraries begin banning it within months. It is a boy and a runaway slave on a raft, going the wrong way down the river he piloted, told from inside the boy's mouth. Life on the Mississippi had gone out the year before with his own river years in it. In a father's library in Palermo, Buenos Aires, a child named Jorge Luis Borges will read this book in English before he reads Don Quixote in Spanish.
stops.quote: The Mississippi is well worth reading about. It is not a commonplace river, but on the contrary is in all ways remarkable.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi (1883), ch. 1 (Project Gutenberg ebook #245)
suggested_refs: The first edition of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, 1884-1885, with E. W. Kemble's illustrations

segments.name: The Machine, the Debt, and the Maid

stops.name: Hartford: the compositor, and the house shut up
stops.date_confidence: month attested for the departure; the Paige investment runs from 1880 to 1894
stops.campa: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court appears in 1889, and most of what it earns goes into the Paige Compositor, a typesetting machine that James Paige keeps almost finishing. Twain puts some three hundred thousand dollars into it across fourteen years, money made by writing about a river fed into a machine built to abolish the type case he was apprenticed to. In June 1891 the Hartford house is closed, the furniture sheeted, the servants let go, and the family sails for Europe because Europe is cheaper. None of them lives there again.
suggested_refs: The Paige Compositor, one surviving machine held at the Mark Twain House, Hartford

stops.name: Florence: the two years of writing
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the Florence residence; the pool dates the villa years 1892-93 without months
stops.campa: The family moves between Berlin, the German spas, and Florence, wherever the exchange rate and Olivia's health allow. In a rented villa outside Florence he writes the Joan of Arc book at last, two years of writing on top of twelve of reading, the whole of it in the voice of an old man remembering: the Sieur Louis de Conte, page and secretary to Joan, born at Neufchateau two years before her. In Paris, Lionel Royer has just painted her in armor before Orleans. The two works are made within a few years of each other by men who never meet.
stops.quote: never done any work before that cost so much thinking and weighing and measuring and planning and cramming
stops.quote_source: Twain to H. H. Rogers on Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc'; given as a fragment because the source gives it as one
suggested_refs: The rented villas of the Florence years, 1892-1893
lionel_royer.journey.json
sources: Wikipedia, 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc'

stops.name: New York: Webster and Company fails
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: Charles L. Webster and Company, the publishing house he founded and largely financed, fails in April, and Twain files for bankruptcy protection. He is fifty-eight, famous on two continents, and owes money to people who trusted his name on a prospectus. The court would discharge the debts at a fraction. He undertakes instead to pay the creditors the whole of what they are owed, and the only asset he has left that can earn on that scale is a man standing alone on a stage, talking.
suggested_refs: The failure of Charles L. Webster and Company, April 1894

stops.name: New York: Harper's prints it without a name
stops.date_confidence: month attested for the start of serialization; the credited book edition follows in May 1896
stops.campa: Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc begins to appear in Harper's Magazine in April, unsigned. Twain has asked for the anonymity because he knows what his name does to a page: a reader who sees Mark Twain on a title page arrives expecting a joke and will find one whether or not it was put there. The serial runs unattributed until the guessing catches up with it, and Harper and Brothers issue the credited book in May 1896. It is the only book he ever published while trying to conceal that he wrote it.
stops.quote: I, THE SIEUR LOUIS DE CONTE, was born in Neufchateau, on the 6th of January, 1410; that is to say, exactly two years before Joan of Arc was born in Domremy.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc (1896), Book I, ch. 1, opening sentence (Project Gutenberg ebook #2874). The corpus reckons de Conte's birth as 1411; the discrepancy stands unresolved
suggested_refs: Harper's Magazine, April 1895 to April 1896, the anonymous serialization

segments.name: Round the World on a Lecture Ticket

stops.name: Sydney: the Australian leg opens
stops.date_confidence: mid-September attested, day unrecorded; the pool wrongly claimed the world tour itself opened here
stops.campa: The tour opened at Cleveland on the fifteenth of July and worked west across the northern states to British Columbia before the Pacific crossing. In September the Australian leg opens at Sydney, to full houses. He is fifty-nine years old and lecturing to clear debts that a court has already offered to forgive him. Australia holds him through the spring, Melbourne after Sydney, and gives the book that follows its convicts, its wildlife, its distances, and its habit of explaining itself to a stranger.
suggested_refs: The Sydney Writers Walk plaque at Circular Quay, marking the 1895 visit

stops.name: Benares: older than tradition
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: He lands at Bombay in January and is knocked sideways by it: the color, the crowding, the noise, more life to the square yard than he has language ready for. At Benares he walks the ghats along the Ganges among the pilgrims washing in the river and the pyres burning at the water's edge, and writes that the city is older than history and older than tradition, and looks it. India takes two months of the tour and rather more than two months of the book.
suggested_refs: The ghats of Benares, described in Following the Equator, chs. 50-52

stops.name: London: the cable about Susy, and the cable about himself
stops.date_confidence: the 1897 London report is attested to the year; Susy Clemens died in August 1896, month traditional in this pool
stops.campa: Susy Clemens dies of spinal meningitis in the shut Hartford house in August 1896, twenty-four years old, while her parents are at sea between South Africa and England. They learn it by cable and Olivia never recovers from it. The tour has cleared the debts. Following the Equator, written in mourning in a rented London house, is published in 1897, and the family goes on to Vienna for two years. In June a reporter calls to check a report that Mark Twain is dead, and leaves with the only line anyone remembers from that summer.
suggested_refs: The New York Journal dispatch of 1897 and the exaggerated report of Twain's death; exact wording not established

stops.name: New York: vice-president of the Anti-Imperialist League
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded
stops.campa: He comes home in 1900 to the reception a country gives a returning general, and spends what is left of his life using it. In 1901 he becomes a vice-president of the American Anti-Imperialist League and writes against the American war in the Philippines, against the argument that a republic can hold a colony and stay a republic. He is sixty-five, out of debt, and no longer under any obligation to be amusing about anything he does not want to be amusing about.
suggested_refs: The American Anti-Imperialist League, 1898-1920, and Twain's vice-presidency from 1901

stops.name: Villa di Quarto, Florence: Olivia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: They lease the Villa di Quarto outside Florence in the autumn of 1903 because the doctors say the climate may hold Olivia a little longer. She is confined to her room and he is allowed in for a few minutes at a time. On the fifth of June 1904 she dies there, fifty-eight years old, thirty-four years married, two of her four children already buried. He takes her home by ship and rail to Elmira and writes nothing of consequence for two years afterwards.
suggested_refs: The Villa di Quarto, Florence, leased 1903-1904

stops.name: Oxford: the scarlet gown
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unrecorded
stops.campa: Oxford gives him an honorary Doctor of Letters and he crosses the Atlantic at seventy-one to collect it in person. He is photographed in the scarlet gown and afterwards wears it on occasions that do not call for a gown at all. The boy who left school after the fifth grade in a Missouri river town, and learned the rest of it standing at a type case in four cities, is a doctor of the oldest university in England. It is his last crossing of the Atlantic.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Encaenia of 1907 and Twain's honorary D.Litt.

stops.name: Stormfield, Redding: the last house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; all three lenses gave wrong coordinates and the corrected value from Wikipedia, 'Stormfield', is used
stops.campa: John Mead Howells builds him a villa on Birch Spray Hill above the Saugatuck valley at Redding, Connecticut, and he moves in on the eighteenth of June 1908. He calls it Stormfield, after a captain in one of his own stories. Clara is away on the concert circuit, Jean is back from years of treatment for her epilepsy, and Olivia has been dead four years. On the thirtieth of November, his seventy-third birthday, sitting in this house, he writes down which of his books he thinks is the best one.
stops.quote: I like the Joan of Arc best of all my books; and it is the best; I know it perfectly well. And besides, it furnished me seven times the pleasure afforded me by any of the others: 12 years of preparation and a years of writing. The others needed no preparation, and got none.
stops.quote_source: Twain's written note of 30 November 1908, reproduced in Albert Bigelow Paine, Mark Twain: A Biography, ch. CXCV (Project Gutenberg ebook #2988); ampersands expanded, and the malformed 'a years of writing' is Twain's own
suggested_refs: Stormfield, Redding, Connecticut, built 1907-1908 by John Mead Howells, burned 1923
sources: Paine, Mark Twain: A Biography, ch. CXCV

stops.name: Stormfield: Jean, on Christmas Eve
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pool's flat 'heart attack' overstates a medical finding that refused to choose
stops.campa: Jean Clemens is found dead in her bath at Stormfield on Christmas Eve, twenty-nine years old. The physicians will not say she drowned: the finding is death not directly from drowning but more probably from strangulation due to epilepsy, or from heart failure. Her father is too ill to travel to the burial at Elmira. He stays in the house and writes the account of the day while the undertakers work downstairs, and calls what he has written the last chapter of his autobiography. He has four months left.
suggested_refs: 'The Death of Jean,' written at Stormfield, 24-26 December 1909

stops.name: Stormfield: he goes out with it
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; Halley's perihelion fell on 20 April 1910
stops.campa: Halley's Comet reaches perihelion on the twentieth of April 1910. On the twenty-first, at Stormfield, Samuel Langhorne Clemens dies of a heart attack, seventy-four years old, one day behind the comet that had passed a fortnight ahead of his birth. He had written the prediction down the year before, in an autobiographical dictation, and the newspapers print it alongside the obituary. He has kept an appointment made seventy-four years in advance with an object in the sky. Two fathoms, and water enough to pass.
stops.quote: I came in with Halley's comet in 1835. It is coming again next year, and I expect to go out with it.
stops.quote_source: Twain's autobiographical dictation of 1909, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Mark Twain'
suggested_refs: Halley's Comet, perihelion 16 November 1835 and 20 April 1910

stops.name: Woodlawn Cemetery, Elmira: twelve feet of stone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; two of the three lenses gave coordinates outside the cemetery and are corrected
stops.campa: He is buried on the twenty-fourth of April in the Langdon plot at Woodlawn Cemetery, beside Olivia, beside Langdon dead at nineteen months, beside Susy dead at twenty-four and Jean dead at twenty-nine, and in time beside Clara, who dies in 1962 having outlived every one of them. Clara sets a monument over the grave twelve feet high, and the height is the whole inscription: twelve feet is two fathoms, and two fathoms is the leadsman's call for water enough to pass.
suggested_refs: The Langdon plot and the twelve-foot Clemens monument, Woodlawn Cemetery, Elmira, on the National Register from 2004

stops.name: Hartford: the house comes off the demolition list
stops.date_confidence: opening year attested; rescue 1929, landmark 1962, restoration begun 1955
stops.campa: By 1929 the house on Farmington Avenue is scheduled for demolition. Katharine Seymour Day raises the money and forms the Mark Twain Memorial to stop it. The building is made a National Historic Landmark in 1962, restored across nineteen years from 1955, and opened to the public as a museum in 1974. The rooms are put back as they stood when the billiard room at the top of the stairs was a workroom and the man in it was writing about a boy on a raft.
suggested_refs: The Mark Twain House and Museum, 351 Farmington Avenue, Hartford

stops.name: Berkeley: the hundred years run out
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded
stops.campa: Twain left instructions that his autobiography, dictated in no order at all and franker than anything he printed, was to stay shut for a hundred years after his death. The Mark Twain Papers at Berkeley keep the terms to the letter. The hundred years run out in April 2010, and in November the University of California Press issues the first volume, over seven hundred pages, a century and seven months after Stormfield. It sells out its printing and goes onto the bestseller lists.
suggested_refs: Autobiography of Mark Twain, vol. 1, University of California Press, November 2010
